title: Is Subsequence
description: Check whether the characters of one string appear in another, in order and with gaps allowed.
statement:
A command palette matches what you typed against a command name when your letters appear in the name in the same order, with other letters allowed in between. Write `is_subsequence(typed, name)` that returns `True` when `typed` is a subsequence of `name` (you can get `typed` by deleting characters from `name`), and `False` otherwise.

- The empty string is a subsequence of every string, including the empty one.
- Each character of `typed` needs a character of `name` of its own, so `"aa"` is not a subsequence of `"a"`.
- Matching is case-sensitive.

**Examples**

```python
is_subsequence("ace", "abcde")   # True
is_subsequence("aec", "abcde")   # False, the letters are there, but not in that order
is_subsequence("", "abc")        # True
```

Aim for one pass over `name`: O(n).
hints: You never need to go back in `name`. What is the least you have to remember while reading it from left to right?
Keep a position in `typed`: the next character you are still waiting for. Read `name` one character at a time, and whenever it equals that character, move the position forward.
You have succeeded exactly when the position has moved past the last character of `typed`. That also makes an empty `typed` work without a special case.
explanation:
**The idea.** Read `name` once, left to right, and keep a position in `typed`: the next character you are still waiting for. Each time `name` shows that character, move the position forward. If you get to the end of `typed`, every character was found, in order.

**Why greedy is enough.** Matching a character of `typed` at its earliest possible place never hurts, because it leaves the longest remaining part of `name` for the rest. So there is nothing to try and nothing to undo.

**Complexity.** O(len(name)) time and O(1) space. Slicing the strings on every step makes it quadratic, and recursing one character at a time runs into Python's recursion limit on a long name.

**A compact form.** `it = iter(name)` followed by `all(ch in it for ch in typed)` does the same: `ch in it` consumes the iterator up to the match, so the next search resumes where this one stopped.

**Follow-up.** With one `name` and many `typed` strings, precompute for every position and letter where that letter occurs next, and each query costs only O(len(typed)).
